newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Moslems give cautious support to Brcko decision.
newsitem.headline: Moslems give cautious support to Brcko decision.

text.p: Bosnian Moslem leaders gave qualified support on Friday to a ruling by an international arbiter over the future of the disputed town of Brcko and they pledged to adhere to the decision.

"It is not just but it is a step towards justice," Alija Izetbegovic, chairman of the Bosnian collective presidency, told reporters. "It is not just because the only just solution was to give Brcko to the (Moslem-Croat) federation."
He had earlier threatened to resign and warned of "chaos" if the strategic town had been awarded to the Serbs.
Saying there were positive and negative aspects of the rulng, Izetbegovic said the authority of an international supervisor for Brkco had not been precisely defined nor was a timetable set out.
"There is a danger that this decision will not be implemented. We have already had very bad experiences with poor implementation," he said.

Izetbegovic, speaking after talks with U.S. envoy John Kornblum and other diplomats from the Contact Group of major powers, praised the ruling for linking the final resolution of the Brcko dispute to the behaviour of the former warring factions.
U.S. arbiter Roberts Owen ruled that neither the Moslem-Croat federation, the Serb republic nor the new inter-ethnic central government was ready to take control over Brcko.

His ruling said a final decision would be made after a year of international supervision. It was possible that Brcko could eventually become a special district outside exclusive control of the Serb and Moslem-Croat entities, he said.
The Serb member of the collective presidency, Momcilo Krajisnik, struck a moderate tone, promising on Bosnian Serb television to work towards a peaceful solution.
Krajisnik said the arbitration process had taken current tensions into account. "We do not whether we reduced tension. We believe we did," he said.
He said "no blackmail and pressures during the arbitration emerged and that all sides should have a positive approach to the problem."
Kornblum said Owen "did not choose to make a final decision but to put in place a process for reducing tensions."
Representatives from the Contact Group -- United States, Britian, France, Germany and Russia -- had flown to Sarajevo to demonstrate their readiness to help to carry out the decision, he added.
Bosnian Foreign Minister Jadranko Prlic, a Croat, said the decision to postpone a final solution was understandable given the current tensions.

"In such an atmosphere it was not easy for the arbiter to make a final decision," Prlic told state radio. "He found a logical way out from the situation and that is to wait how things will develop within the next year."
But political analysts in Sarajevo expressed scepticism about a decision which relied on the goodwill of the former warring factions.
Similar plans to reunify the divided town of Mostar under European Union administration failed, in part because there was no leverage over recalcitrant authorities to ensure they kept their promises.
